title: Lutherans and Catholics (2016)
hookLine: Pope Francis went to Sweden to mark the Reformation's anniversary with Lutherans

cards: An anniversary of a split is an odd thing to mark together. The Reformation began with Martin Luther, a German friar, and it ended with Christians in the West divided, and for long stretches, at war.
So when the anniversary came around, a real question hung in the air: should Catholics and Lutherans mark it separately, one side celebrating and the other mourning?
Pope Francis answered by getting on a plane to Lund, in Sweden, to mark it with Lutherans in their own cathedral.

teach.b: Day seven hundred eighty-two looked at what the reformers asked. Today, the day the split was remembered together. The service in Lund wasn't a party, and it wasn't a funeral.

Catholic and Lutheran leaders prayed together in a common service built around thanksgiving, repentance and commitment: thanks for the gifts each church has received, sorrow for the wounds each has caused the other, and a promise to keep walking together.
Pope Francis and the president of the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint statement there.
Both sides gave thanks for the theological gifts of the Reformation, asked forgiveness for hurts and violence between them, and committed to common witness and service to the poor.
They also said, honestly, that they still can't share the Eucharist at one altar, and they named the pain of people who share their whole lives but not that table. Now the words in your line.

From Conflict to Communion is the title of a report by the Lutheran and Catholic commission for unity, written so both churches could tell the story of the Reformation together, with both sides' memories in view.

Behind it lies an older agreement, the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, where both churches said they share a common understanding of basic truths about how God makes sinners right with him.
Lund asked two families with a painful past to tell their story in one voice, without pretending it didn't hurt.

how: Catholics and Lutherans continue an official international dialogue, and in some places hold joint prayer services, especially around Reformation Day and the week of prayer for Christian unity.

practice: Let a Lutheran church, or a Lutheran you know, come to mind, or a family where one spouse is Catholic and the other Lutheran, sitting apart at the moment of communion.
If you pray, pray for them, and for the day both churches hope for, when they can share one altar. If you don't pray, hold them in mind with goodwill.
